body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Case management for frequent emergency department users: a systematic review of effects on visits and costs","authors":"Harrington-Oyelaran P, Veld-Nakamura S, Castaneda-Boateng R","year":2019,"venue":"Emergency Medicine Reviews","doi":"10.5555/emr.2019.0712","providerType":"review","abstract":"We identified 31 studies of case management for adults who frequently attend emergency departments, 5 of them randomised trials. Most reported fewer emergency visits after enrolment, but the before-after studies could not separate the programme from regression to the mean, and the randomised trials found smaller reductions (median 12 percent). Only 6 studies reported mortality or intensive care admission, with inconsistent results. Programme content, caseloads and definitions of frequent use varied widely. The authors call for evaluations of hard outcomes that account for regression to the mean."},{"title":"Mortality and intensive care admission among frequent emergency department attenders: a regional linkage study","authors":"Ferreira-Lindahl M, Oduro-Kaspar J","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Emergency Care Outcomes","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Linking regional emergency department and hospital data for 8,900 adults with eight or more visits in a year, we found 12-month mortality of 3.4 percent and intensive care admission of 2.9 percent, together affecting 6.0 percent of frequent attenders. Risk was highest among those with heart failure, chronic lung disease or alcohol dependence, and among people with no family doctor. Frequent attenders were younger than other patients with the same outcomes. The authors suggest that services for frequent attenders should be judged on these outcomes, not only on visit counts."},{"title":"Case management enrolment and 12-month death or intensive care admission in frequent attenders: a matched case-control study at one urban emergency department","authors":"Nwankwo-Stead L, Bergmann-Achebe T, Iyer-Fontaine C","year":2023,"venue":"Acute and Emergency Care","doi":"10.5555/aec.2023.0438","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We identified 64 frequent attenders who died or were admitted to intensive care within 12 months of an index visit and matched four controls to each on age, sex and index month. Case management enrolment before the index date was less common among cases (odds ratio 0.62, 95 percent CI 0.38 to 1.01) after adjustment for prior visits and comorbidity. The estimate was imprecise because of the small number of cases, and enrolment favoured patients with social rather than medical needs. The authors recommend a multi-site study with more cases."},{"title":"Confounding by indication in evaluations of case management: enrolment favours the most complex patients","authors":"Kowalczyk-Amadi R, Thorsen-Mbeki E","year":2018,"venue":"Health Services Methods Notes","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using data from four case management programmes, we compared patients enrolled with eligible patients not enrolled. Enrolled patients had more emergency visits in the previous year (median 14 against 10), more mental health diagnoses and more housing instability. Without adjustment for these factors, enrolment appeared to double the risk of death; after adjustment for prior visit count and a comorbidity index, the association reversed. The authors recommend matching or adjusting on prior utilisation and measuring exposure only before the outcome date."},{"title":"Measuring exposure to case management from care plan files: agreement between two abstractors","authors":"Solberg-Nnamdi A, Pereira-Hollis D","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Care Management Research","doi":"10.5555/jcmr.2020.0156","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two trained abstractors independently read 150 case management files to record enrolment date, number of case manager contacts and care plan content. Agreement on enrolment date within 14 days was excellent (kappa 0.81), but agreement on the number of contacts was moderate (weighted kappa 0.58) because contacts were recorded in several places. Reading a file took a median of 44 minutes. The authors recommend using enrolment date as the main exposure and treating contact counts as a secondary exposure with a written abstraction guide."},{"title":"Variation in frequent attender case management across community and tertiary emergency departments","authors":"Mbatha-Laurent J, Okafor-Sandvik H","year":2024,"venue":"Emergency Services Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared case management programmes for frequent attenders at 12 emergency departments. Caseloads ranged from 35 to 80 patients per case manager, and community departments more often relied on nurses than social workers. Enrolment criteria differed: 8 departments used a visit threshold alone and 4 added clinical judgement. Median time from eligibility to enrolment was 3 weeks at tertiary and 9 weeks at community departments. The authors suggest that multi-site evaluations match or stratify by site because programme intensity differs."},{"title":"Incidence density sampling of controls for time-varying programme exposure","authors":"Lindqvist-Obi F, Marchetti-Ansah K","year":2016,"venue":"Epidemiological Methods Letters","doi":"10.5555/eml.2016.0033","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"When exposure to a programme changes over time, controls sampled from people who never had the outcome can bias a case-control estimate. We show with simulated data that sampling controls from those still at risk at each case's event date (incidence density sampling) recovers the true rate ratio, whereas sampling from survivors to the end of follow-up overstated a protective effect by up to 30 percent. Exposure must be measured before each matched set's index date. The approach applies directly to enrolment in case management and similar programmes."}]}
